title: Strongly convex lower level: stochastic gradients and derivative-vector products
summary: Solve the bilevel problem $\min_x\Phi(x)$, where $\Phi(x)=f(x,y^*(x))$ and $y^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_y g(x,y)$ is the unique global lower-level solution. The upper- and lower-level variables are $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}$ and $y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}$. Seek approximate stationarity of the reduced objective under the declared criterion and guarantee; assumptions on $f$, $g$, and $\Phi$ are specified separately.

description_paragraphs: Solve the bilevel problem $\min_x\Phi(x)$, where $\Phi(x)=f(x,y^*(x))$ and $y^*(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_y g(x,y)$ is the unique global lower-level solution. The upper- and lower-level variables are $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d_x}$ and $y\in\mathbb{R}^{d_y}$. Seek approximate stationarity of the reduced objective under the declared criterion and guarantee; assumptions on $f$, $g$, and $\Phi$ are specified separately.
The population functions are $f=\mathbb E_\xi F(\cdot;\xi)$ and $g=\mathbb E_\zeta G(\cdot;\zeta)$. Upper- and lower-level sample seeds are denoted by $\xi,\zeta$.

model.instance: (f,g,x0,y0) and declared oracle law; dimensions are arbitrary finite and minimax is over them

assumptions.description: For every fixed upper-level point $x$, the function $g(x,·)$ is $\mu$-strongly convex on all of $\mathbb R^{d_y}$. Convexity in $x$ or joint convexity in $(x,y)$ is not assumed.

The population full gradient $
abla f=(
abla_x f,
abla_y f)$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz in $(x,y)$. Convexity of $f$ is not required.

The population full gradient $
abla g=(
abla_x g,
abla_y g)$ is globally $L$-Lipschitz in $(x,y)$.
The objective $\Phi$ has a finite lower bound. A point $x_0$ is given and satisfies $\Phi(x_0)-\inf_x\Phi(x)\le\Delta$. Convexity or existence of a global minimizer of $\Phi$ is not required.
The initial point $(x_0,y_0)$ and bound $\|y_0-y^*(x_0)\|\le R_0$ are given. This is an initialization budget, not a requirement that the oracle return $y^*$.
The function $f$ is jointly $M$-Lipschitz in the full variable $(x,y)$. This budget is recorded as $C_f=M$ and therefore bounds the full gradient. It is stronger than a bound only on $f_y$.
The function $g_{xy}$ is $\tau$-Lipschitz in $(x,y)$, and $g_{yy}$ is $\rho$-Lipschitz. These budgets are specified separately and are not combined into an unspecified common constant.
For almost every upper-level sample xi, $F(\cdot;\xi)$ is jointly $M=C_f$-Lipschitz and $\nabla F$ is jointly $L$-Lipschitz, with constants uniform over all samples.

For almost every lower-level sample, $G(x,\cdot;\zeta)$ is $\mu$-strongly convex; $\nabla G$ is jointly $L$-Lipschitz, and the joint Lipschitz budgets for $G_{xy}$ and $G_{yy}$ are $\tau,\rho$. These bounds hold uniformly over samples.

The population quantities are sample expectations, and the derivative estimates are unbiased. The condition $\mathbb E\|\nabla G-\nabla g\|^2\le\sigma^2$ holds at every point and remains valid conditionally on the history before a fresh draw. This is not an unbiasedness assertion for each fixed sample.

oracle.query_domain_description: Upper and lower points may be selected adaptively throughout their declared Euclidean spaces. Each operation specifies direction dimensions and control over samples or indices.
oracle.native_source_protocol: Ji et al. (2021), Definition 2 on PDF p. 5, count partial gradients separately. In Algorithms 2–3, stocBiO approximates the inverse action using HVPs, each of which is charged.
description_paragraphs: Public inputs include dimension, target accuracy, quantitative model budgets, and initial points. Functions, lower-level optimizers, and the reduced objective are hidden.

Upper-level interface: choose $b\in\{x,y\}$ and $(x,y)$ and receive $\nabla_b F(x,y;\xi)$. The two partial gradients at the same fixed point may share an upper-level sample, but are charged separately.

For a lower-level gradient query, choose $b\in\{x,y\}$ and $(x,y)$ and return $\nabla_bG(x,y;\zeta)$ from a fresh lower-level sample. Each partial gradient lies in the space of its corresponding variable block.
Cross-Hessian vector product: $(x,y,v)\mapsto G_{xy}(x,y;\zeta)v\in\mathbb R^{d_x}$, where $v\in\mathbb R^{d_y}$, using a fresh lower-level sample.
Hessian–vector products take the form $(x,y,v)\mapsto G_{yy}(x,y;\zeta)v\in\mathbb R^{d_y}$, where $v\in\mathbb R^{d_y}$. Each product uses a fresh lower-level sample.

Queries may use the entire joint Euclidean space. Every fresh draw is conditionally unbiased given the history before that draw. The second upper-level partial gradient from the same sample is unbiased only relative to the history preceding that sample. Lower-level updates, cross-derivative products, and Neumann-series product batches are independent. The interface does not permit reuse of a sample at different points.

metric.normalization: The tolerance is on the gradient-norm scale. This contract requires $\mathbb E\|\nabla\Phi\|^2\le\epsilon^2$.
metric.finiteness_conditions: Guaranteed by the model and the associated differentiability result, not inferred from an oracle-order label alone.
description_paragraphs: The base error is $\|\nabla\Phi(\widehat{x})\|_2^2$. The tolerance $\varepsilon$ is always expressed on the gradient-norm scale. The mean-square requirement is equivalent to the RMS gradient being at most this tolerance.

abla_y g$, and $y^*$ denotes $y^*(x)$. The identity defines the hypergradient without granting additional query access.

resource.budget_semantics: fixed worst-case total number of calls on every execution
resource.scalarization: Retain the four-dimensional feasible resource vector (N_grad_f, N_grad_g, N_JVP, N_HVP). Each partial gradient, JVP, or HVP costs one unit in its own coordinate. Solving an entire internal linear system is not a single primitive call.
resource.setup_cost: Initialization oracle calls count toward the total. A finite initialization bound is an instance-class assumption, not free access to an inner solver.
resource.precision_model: Exact real arithmetic is assumed; the stochastic oracle has the stated noise. Bit complexity, memory, and arithmetic cost are not tracked.
description_paragraphs: Retain the joint budget $(N_{\nabla f},N_{\nabla g},N_J,N_H)$, counting sampled F-partial gradients, sampled G-partial gradients, cross-Hessian vector products, and Hessian-vector products separately. Each sample response increments its coordinate by one; a batch is not a free bundled call.
Initialization oracle calls count toward the total. A finite initialization bound is an instance-class assumption, not free access to an inner solver.
The budget is a fixed worst-case cap on every execution path; every actual response within a batch is counted.

Internal processing of available information is free. Comparisons use the explicitly specified scalarization or resource vector. Different resources without given weights cannot be assembled coordinatewise from separate algorithms.

algorithms.adaptivity: arbitrary measurable functions of past responses
algorithms.internal_computation: This model counts only oracle resources. Arithmetic, linear algebra, and storage applied to received responses are free. Any extra hidden-function gradient, HVP/JVP, value, or inner-solve response must be obtained through a declared, charged operation.
algorithms.parallelism: sequential adaptive calls; simultaneous batch calls count separately
description_paragraphs: Algorithms may use private randomness. Queries, stopping, and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable functions of the transcript. The output may be unqueried, a random selection of a past point, or an admissible average. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed. Queries are sequential; each actual response in a parallel batch is charged separately. Arithmetic, linear algebra, and storage using received data are uncharged. Internal operations, memory, and communication are not tracked by this quantity.

aggregation_order: For each fixed admissible instance, first take expectation over oracle noise and private algorithmic randomness. The resulting guarantee must hold for every admissible instance.
guarantees.quantifier_order: A single algorithm family, depending only on public budgets and the interaction history, must meet the target for every admissible function and oracle law. Minimax quantifiers are infimum over algorithms followed by supremum over instances; the algorithm is not selected separately for each hidden instance.

bounds.parameter_choice: as cited theorem; any reparameterization is recorded under derivation

applicability.dimension_conditions: Valid in every finite dimension of the declared model. No additional dimension dependence is introduced beyond the formula.
applicability.guarantee_mapping: The source uses $\varepsilon$ for squared-gradient tolerance. Write it as $\eta_{\rm src}$ to avoid ambiguity and substitute $\eta_{\rm src}=\varepsilon^2$ consistently. The target here is $\mathbb E\|\nabla\Phi(\widehat x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$.
applicability.oracle_mapping: Sampled F/G partial gradients and stochastic Jacobian/Hessian-vector products satisfy the stated samplewise regularity and fresh-sample conditional unbiasedness conditions. Same-sample coupling follows the oracle protocol and does not permit unrestricted reuse across points. Each partial gradient or vector product is charged separately; no inner-solve primitive is available.
applicability.output_mapping: After the prescribed K iterations, draw $R\in\{0,\ldots,K-1\}$ independently and uniformly, and return $\widehat x=x_R$. The bound on the average squared gradient becomes an expected squared-gradient bound for this output; the same guarantee is not claimed for the last iterate.
applicability.resource_mapping: Charged resources are $N_{\nabla f}$, $N_{\nabla g}$, $N_J$, and $N_H$, with a fixed worst-case cap per execution. All four bounds hold simultaneously. There is no free inner-solve operation; its primitive queries count in the corresponding coordinates.

bounds.hidden_constants: In the accuracy asymptotics, hold regularity, initialization, and noise budgets fixed while allowing dimension to vary. Condition-number powers are reported as in the source theorem and do not certify joint optimality. The source inner-loop lengths contain condition-number logarithms, so the relevant resource coordinates retain soft-O notation.
hidden_logs: The inner-loop length contains $\log(2+\kappa)$. The Hessian-vector-product coordinate also contains $\log(2+\kappa^2/\varepsilon^2)$ from truncating the Neumann series; the source suppresses this factor in tilde notation.
bounds.derivation: Apply the same substitution $\eta_{\rm src}=\varepsilon^2$ simultaneously to every resource coordinate of the source algorithm. Independently select a historical outer iterate uniformly for output. This conversion preserves the four-dimensional joint budget.
